title: The retry that ate the recovery
subtitle: Classification, jitter, budgets and the five ways a retry stops, read against what resilience libraries ship in October 2026

sources.title: Google Cloud Service Health incident ow5i3PPK96RduMcb1SsW: multiple GCP products returned 503 errors (full Incident Report)
sources.took: the opening incident: a null-pointer crash loop in Service Control on 2025-06-12 whose restarts overloaded Spanner because, in Google's own words, randomized exponential backoff was not implemented, and 'It took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve in us-central-1'; the page header dates the disruption 10:51 to 18:18 US/Pacific while the earlier Mini Incident Report on the same page gives 10:49 to 13:49. Recounted 2026-10-14: the Full Incident Report's 'What's our approach moving forward?' list carries SEVEN items (not eight), the fifth being 'We will audit and ensure our systems employ randomized exponential backoff'; the Mini Incident Report's 'Additional details' adds three further prevention items, and a change freeze on the Service Control stack is listed as an immediate action rather than a forward item

sources.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
sources.took: retry amplification in 'a five-deep stack of service calls' with 'three retries at each layer' where 'the load on the database will increase 243x, making it unlikely to ever recover', the token-bucket retry quota, idempotency as the precondition for retrying writes, the best practice to 'retry at a single point in the stack' for low-cost operations, and the vendor's own argument that 'circuit breakers introduce modal behavior into systems that can be difficult to test' and can significantly lengthen recovery. Re-read 2026-10-14 for the attempt wording: the prose says 'three retries at each layer' while its own walk-through counts 'first three tries, then nine tries', and 3^5 = 243, so the multiplier is three attempts per layer

sources.title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
sources.took: the original simulation comparing no backoff, capped exponential backoff, full jitter, equal jitter and decorrelated jitter, including that total work still grows as N squared in that simulated contention model and that equal jitter ranks last among the jittered variants (history, updated 2023-05)

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 21: Handling Overload
sources.took: client-side adaptive throttling with a 2x accept multiplier over a two-minute window, the three-attempt per-request limit, the 10 percent per-client retry budget, the resulting growth figures (just under 3x, reduced to about 1.1x for one client's own traffic in the worst-case scenario), and the counter-conventional rule to retry only at the layer immediately above the rejecting layer

sources.title: gRFC A6: gRPC Retry Design
sources.took: the retry throttling token bucket (maxTokens up to 1000, failures minus 1, successes plus tokenRatio, retries suppressed at or below maxTokens/2), the client-side cap of 5 attempts ('Values greater than 5 are treated as 5 without being considered a validation error', and 'This client-side maximum value can be changed by the client through the use of channel arguments'), the backoff formula with unconditional random(0.8, 1.2) jitter applied outside the maxBackoff cap, retryableStatusCodes, the hedging policy, and the grpc-retry-pushback-ms server override that resets the ladder. Re-read 2026-10-14 for deadlines: 'gRPC's call deadline applies across all attempts for a given RPC', the operation fails once the deadline passes 'regardless of how many attempts were configured or attempted', 'As with retries, gRPC call deadlines apply to the entire chain of hedged requests', transparent retries run 'until a success occurs, or the RPC's deadline passes', and the document is silent on a deadline expiring mid-backoff and on deadlines in the pushback section

sources.title: Retry behavior (AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide)
sources.took: the 2026 retry behaviour, which the page's own Important box gates: 'The behavior described on this page requires opting in until it becomes the default behavior. Set AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true in your environment.' Three-way error classification (transient, throttling, non-retryable) with 50 ms and 1000 ms base delays, delay = random(0,1) x min(20000 ms, base x 2^retry), 3 default max attempts (4 for DynamoDB at a 25 ms base), the 500-token quota costing 14 per transient and 5 per throttling retry, the roughly 22 and 32 percent sustained-failure rates at which the quota starts to drain, the x-amz-retry-after clamp, and forced backoff for long-polling operations. Re-read 2026-10-14 for the documented status fallback: the transient table's last row is '(any HTTP 500, 502, 503, or 504 without a recognized error code)', the throttling class is a list of 14 error codes with no documented status-code fallback, and the note 'The SDK matches on error code first, then falls back to HTTP status code'; the worked examples give about 75 ms average added latency for a transient error and about 1,500 ms for throttling at 3 attempts (page carries no publication date)

sources.title: Announcing updated retry behavior for AWS SDKs and Tools
sources.took: that the new behaviour is opt-in via AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026 and becomes the default in November 2026, that per-SDK base delays previously ranged from 10 ms to 1000 ms with inconsistent quotas, and the stated reasons (some SDKs waited too long on transient errors, others kept retrying through sustained outages)

sources.title: Circuit breakers (Envoy v3 API reference, build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06)
sources.took: the retry budget as a concurrency bound: budget_percent default 20 percent of active plus pending requests, min_retry_concurrency default 3, the max_retries circuit breaker default of 3 that the budget overrides, and the note that remaining retry capacity is then not tracked in stats (docs build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06, read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Outlier detection (Envoy v3 API reference, build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06)
sources.took: per-host breaker defaults: consecutive_5xx 5, interval 10 s, base_ejection_time 30 s, max_ejection_percent 10 percent, max_ejection_time 300 s, success_rate_request_volume 100 over at least 5 hosts with a 1.9 standard-deviation factor, and failure_percentage enforcement off by default (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Outlier detection (Envoy architecture overview)
sources.took: that ejection is per host, capped by max_ejection_percent, that ejection time is base_ejection_time multiplied by consecutive ejections up to max_ejection_time, that the multiplier decays one step per interval while healthy, and that panic mode can still route to ejected hosts (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Getting started with resilience4j-circuitbreaker
sources.took: the documented breaker defaults: CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN plus METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED and FORCED_OPEN; count-based sliding window of 100; failureRateThreshold 50 percent; minimumNumberOfCalls 100; waitDurationInOpenState 60 s; permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, whose failure and slow-call rates are evaluated rather than required to pass; slowCallDurationThreshold 60 s; and automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled false, so the probe happens only when a call arrives (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Getting started with resilience4j-retry
sources.took: the documented retry defaults: maxAttempts 3 and a constant waitDuration of 500 ms with no randomization, with IntervalFunction.ofExponentialBackoff() and IntervalFunction.ofRandomized() as opt-in helpers (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Releases, resilience4j/resilience4j
sources.took: the version the defaults above belong to: v2.4.0 listed as the latest release on the read date

sources.title: Circuit breaker resilience strategy (Polly documentation)
sources.took: the documented breaker defaults: FailureRatio 0.1, MinimumThroughput 100 executions inside a SamplingDuration of 30 s, BreakDuration 5 s, a single probe execution in half-open, and that the transition to half-open happens only when Execute is called, so a caller that skips broken circuits never probes (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Retry resilience strategy (Polly documentation)
sources.took: the documented retry defaults: MaxRetryAttempts 3, Delay 2 s, BackoffType Constant, MaxDelay null and UseJitter false, with exponential-plus-jitter implemented as Decorrelated Jitter Backoff V2 when enabled (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Releases, App-vNext/Polly
sources.took: the version the defaults above belong to: 8.8.0 listed as the latest release on the read date

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, section 9.2.2 (Idempotent Methods) and section 10.2.3 (Retry-After)
sources.took: the Retry-After grammar (HTTP-date or delay-seconds, 'a non-negative decimal integer, representing time in seconds'), that servers send it 'to indicate how long the user agent ought to wait', and that the section gives its meaning only for 503 ('how long the service is expected to be unavailable to the client') and for 3xx ('the minimum time that the user agent is asked to wait before issuing the redirected request'), with no mention of 429. Read 2026-10-14 for section 9.2.2: 'Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response'; 'A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent, regardless of the method, or some means to detect that the original request was never applied'; 'A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests.'

sources.title: RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes, section 4 (429 Too Many Requests)
sources.took: that 429 is defined here and that the response MAY include Retry-After, so a rate-limited client is not guaranteed a stated delay (history)

sources.title: RateLimit header fields for HTTP, draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-11
sources.took: the RateLimit field (r for remaining quota, t for the effective window in seconds, pk for partition key) and RateLimit-Policy parameters, the rule that Retry-After MUST take precedence over RateLimit, that the spec mandates no retry algorithm, that delay-seconds rather than timestamps mitigates thundering herd, and section 8.5's own advice to add jitter to the effective window because clients otherwise return at the same instant

sources.title: draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers (IETF Datatracker document page)
sources.took: the stressed absence claim: the RateLimit header fields are still an active Internet-Draft at revision 11, IESG state I-D Exists, expiring 2026-11-24, so there is no published RFC for them as of the read date (the page's intended-status metadata field is weak evidence about the working group's plan and is not used)

sources.title: draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header (IETF Datatracker document page)
sources.took: that the Idempotency-Key header draft, whose abstract offers fault tolerance for non-idempotent methods such as POST and PATCH, reached revision 07 on 2025-10-15 and is now in IESG state Expired, so the precondition for safely retrying a write has no finished standard

sources.title: KEP-4603: Tune CrashLoopBackOff
sources.took: the kubelet's restart ladder (10 s, 20 s, 40 s, capped at 5 minutes, reset only after 10 minutes of healthy running), the benchmark on 110 instantly crashing single-container pods on one node (pod API traffic peaking near the kubelet's ~5 QPS client limit, runtime CPU about 10x, kubelet and API server CPU about 2x), the alpha proposal to cut the ladder to 1 s initial and 60 s maximum behind the ReduceDefaultCrashLoopBackOffDecay gate (spelling per [40]), the modelled estimate of about 5 extra restarts per crashing pod in the first five minutes, and the counter-argument that some restart throttling is always needed for node stability

sources.title: KEP-5593: Configure the max CrashLoopBackOff delay
sources.took: that the unchanged default ladder is 10 s doubling to a 300 s cap, that operators can now opt into a per-node maximum of 1 to 300 s behind the KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax gate (beta at v1.35), the stress test in which a 0 second maximum raised API server QPS up to 30x, and the stated risk that a 1 s maximum costs roughly 10x more pod state-transition API requests on a saturated node (field spelling verified against the shipped reference [37])

sources.title: Metastable Failures in the Wild (OSDI '22)
sources.took: 22 metastable failures studied in depth 'from 11 different organizations', and that 'at least 4 out of 15 major outages in the last decade at Amazon Web Services were caused by metastable failures'. Abstract re-read 2026-10-14: the page credits the framework to prior work ('Recently, Bronson et al. introduced a framework...') and says the authors 'extend the model by Bronson et al.' by 'categorizing two types of triggers and two types of amplification mechanisms', so the page itself does not define the vulnerable-state, trigger and sustaining-effect model and names amplification mechanisms beyond retry machinery

sources.title: Will circuit breakers solve my problems?
sources.took: the central objection: in sharded and cell-based systems failure is partial, so a breaker that trips on one shard's failures punishes callers of healthy shards and a breaker that does not trip does nothing, and clients cannot predict whether a specific call will succeed without knowing server internals

sources.title: Fixing retries with token buckets and circuit breakers
sources.took: the simulation of one failing service with 100 independent Poisson clients: three retries cost 1+N (four) times the work at a 100 percent failure rate, and in that main 100-client model 'the breaker strategy starts tripping a little early: around half the expected rate'. Re-read 2026-10-14: in the runs that split the same total traffic across 10, 100 and 1,000 clients the breaker 'is tripping too early, and approaching the performance of the no retries approach' while the bucket 'doesn't deplete its bucket fast enough, converging on the behavior of n retries'; of the token bucket the author writes 'The adaptive strategy isn't modal in the same way, and seems to perform better at lower failure rates, but does give some (tunable) additional load at higher rates'

sources.title: Retry Amplification in Distributed Systems: A Systematic Analysis of Retry Policies and Their Role in Cascading Failures
sources.took: the strongest counter-evidence, from the abstract page: across 200 open-source Python microservice projects, explicit retry logic detected in 11.5 percent (authors estimate true prevalence near 41 percent after auditing false negatives), 60.9 percent of detected projects carrying at least one configuration with no backoff, exactly 1 of 113 manually verified production configurations randomizing its delay, the retry amplification factor metric, five anti-patterns, and a simulation (100 trials per strategy) where a naive retry policy cut the success rate to 41.5 percent against 55.4 percent with no retries at all; the abstract page carries no circuit-breaker or budgeting figures, which are in the full text [39]

sources.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1)
sources.took: the second incident: a DNS Enactor delayed while retrying endpoint updates 'applied its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan', after which 'The second Enactor's clean-up process then deleted this older plan because it was many generations older than the plan it had just applied' and 'As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed'; DWFM 'had entered a state of congestive collapse and was unable to make forward progress in recovering droplet leases' with 'Additional work was queued to reattempt establishing the droplet lease', engineers throttled incoming work at 04:14 PDT, and the remediation promises to 'rate limit incoming work based on the size of the waiting queue' in EC2 data propagation. Re-read 2026-10-14: the summary states the Enactor 'will retry each endpoint until the plan is successfully applied' but gives no retry interval, spacing or backoff anywhere

sources.title: Semantic conventions for HTTP spans
sources.took: the one standard retry signal in the HTTP conventions: http.request.resend_count, stable, 'the ordinal number of request resending attempt (for any reason, including redirects)', recommended if and only if the request was retried, counted regardless of cause (redirects, auth challenges, 503, network issues); links point to specification v1.59.0 (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Semantic conventions for HTTP metrics
sources.took: the stressed absence claim, scoped to the HTTP conventions: the six HTTP client metrics defined (request.duration, request.body.size, response.body.size, open_connections, connection.duration, active_requests) carry no retry, resend or attempt attribute, and searching the page for 'resend', 'retry' and 'attempt' returns no match as of the read date

sources.title: Retry Policies (Temporal documentation)
sources.took: a durable-retry default: Activities retry automatically with a 1 s initial interval, 2.0 backoff coefficient, maximum interval of 100x the initial and unlimited maximum attempts, Workflow Executions carry no retry policy by default, Workflow Task retries back off outside the policy up to 10 minutes, non-retryable error types are matched on the failure type, and a pending Activity's attempt count is visible through Describe while attempts stay out of Event History until the Activity ends (page carries no date; read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Netflix/Hystrix (repository README)
sources.took: labelled history: 'Hystrix is no longer in active development, and is currently in maintenance mode', final release 1.5.18, with Netflix pointing new internal projects at resilience4j and at adaptive implementations that react to real-time performance such as adaptive concurrency limits (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS
sources.took: the terminal destination: maxReceiveCount as the number of receives before a message moves to the dead-letter queue, and the warning that a value of 1 dead-letters on a single failed receive (page carries no date; read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems (HotOS 2021 record)
sources.publisher: Penn State Pure research record (Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko, Zhu)
sources.took: the attribution the post needs for the metastable-failure framework that [24] extends: Nathan Bronson, Abutalib Aghayev, Aleksey Charapko and Timothy Zhu, 'Metastable failures in distributed systems', HotOS 2021 (18th Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems), ACM, pages 221 to 227, doi 10.1145/3458336.3465286, which introduces the framework, applies it to examples from operating large-scale systems, treats these failures as black swan events and leaves robustness to unknown metastable failures as an open problem. The paper PDF has no extractable text layer and the ACM page returns 403, so this bibliographic record is what was opened (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Metastability and Distributed Systems
sources.took: the mechanism statement the post rests the amplification argument on: 'a trigger causes the system to enter a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed', examples of triggers (a short failure, a spike of load, a deployment), 'We consider the root cause of a metastable failure to be the sustaining feedback loop, rather than the trigger', a 'stable down' state in which clients keep sending work and goodput is zero, and that retries make systems more vulnerable by 'converting small outages into sudden (and metastable) periods of internal retry storms', lowering the everyday error rate while raising exposure to this failure mode (date from the post's URL path; read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Panic threshold (Envoy architecture overview, load balancing)
sources.took: the condition under which per-host ejection helps and where it stops: the panic threshold defaults to 50 percent, below which Envoy stops using health status and balances across all hosts (or none, depending on mode), existing to 'avoid a situation in which host failures cascade throughout the cluster as load increases'; setting it to 0 percent disables panic mode for a priority level, and failing traffic reduces load on a struggling upstream at the cost of requests that never succeed (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Kubelet Configuration (v1beta1) API reference, CrashLoopBackOffConfig
sources.took: the shipped field spelling for the code block: KubeletConfiguration carries a crashLoopBackOff field of type CrashLoopBackOffConfig, 'CrashLoopBackOff contains config to modify node-level parameters for container restart behavior', whose single field is maxContainerRestartPeriod of type meta/v1.Duration, 'the maximum duration the backoff delay can accrue to for container restarts, minimum 1 second, maximum 300 seconds. If not set, defaults to the internal crashloopbackoff maximum (300s)'; the reference section names no feature gate (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: OpenTelemetry Metrics (gRPC documentation)
sources.took: the counter-evidence to a general claim about missing retry telemetry: gRPC defines stable per-attempt client instruments (grpc.client.attempt.started, grpc.client.attempt.duration, grpc.client.attempt.sent_total_compressed_message_size, grpc.client.attempt.rcvd_total_compressed_message_size) beside the stable per-call grpc.client.call.duration, plus four experimental per-call retry instruments (grpc.client.call.retries, grpc.client.call.transparent_retries, grpc.client.call.hedges, grpc.client.call.retry_delay), and states that 'Experimental metrics are always off by default' (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Retry Amplification in Distributed Systems (full text, v1)
sources.took: the results and limits the abstract omits: Tables III and IV, 100 trials per configuration on one 5-tier linear chain (API, Auth, Catalog, Inventory, Database) at 50 percent baseline utilization, with scenario S3 success rates of 55.4 percent no retry, 41.5 percent standard retry (3 attempts, exponential backoff of 100, 200 and 400 ms, with jitter), 55.3 percent for standard retry plus a circuit breaker tripping at a 50 percent failure rate and staying open 30 s, and 54.9 percent for Adaptive Retry Budgeting (initial budget 0.2 of base load, alpha 0.1, beta 0.5, high and low thresholds 0.3 and 0.05, window 1.0 s, backpressure above 80 percent queue or 90 percent CPU); retry amplification factors 1.34 for standard retry against 1.00 to 1.01 for the other three; and section VIII-B's limits, a single topology, an idealized network, independent probabilistic failures, synchronous calls only, and an analytical bound of 10.30x against 1.34x simulated that the authors say should not be read as a forecast (read 2026-10-14)

sources.title: Feature Gates (Kubernetes reference)
sources.took: the shipped status of the two separate features: KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax is alpha and default false from 1.32 to 1.34 and beta and default true since 1.35, while ReduceDefaultCrashLoopBackOffDecay (that spelling) is alpha and default false since 1.33, described as enabling 'reduction of both the initial delay and the maximum delay accrued between container restarts for a node for containers in CrashLoopBackOff across the cluster to 1s initial delay and 60s maximum delay' (read 2026-10-14)

claims.text: On 2025-06-12 at about 10:45 PDT a policy change with unintended blank fields was inserted into the regional Spanner tables Google Cloud's Service Control uses for policies, replicated globally within seconds, and hit a null pointer that put the Service Control binaries into a crash loop in every region.

Google's incident report for 2025-06-12 states that the red-button rollout disabling the faulty serving path was completed within 40 minutes of the incident, with recovery starting in the smaller regions first.

Google's incident report for 2025-06-12 states, of the larger regions, that restarting Service Control tasks overloaded the underlying Spanner table and that 'Service Control did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented to avoid this'.

Google's incident report for 2025-06-12 states that 'It took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve in us-central-1', because engineers throttled task creation and routed traffic to multi-regional databases to reduce load on the underlying infrastructure; the report states no counterfactual recovery time for a Service Control that had backoff.

The Google Cloud incident dashboard dates the 2025-06-12 disruption, increased 503 errors across multiple Google Cloud products, from 10:51 to 18:18 US/Pacific; the earlier Mini Incident Report on the same page gives a 3-hour window (10:49 to 13:49), which does not match the dashboard end time.

Recounted on the page on 2026-10-14: Google's full incident report for 2025-06-12 publishes seven forward-looking items under 'What's our approach moving forward?', among them 'We will audit and ensure our systems employ randomized exponential backoff', modularizing Service Control so functionality is isolated and fails open, auditing all systems that consume globally replicated data, and enforcing feature-flag protection disabled by default for changes to critical binaries; the earlier Mini Incident Report on the same page adds three prevention items, and the change freeze on the Service Control stack is listed as an immediate action rather than a forward item.

The Amazon Builders' Library describes 'a five-deep stack of service calls' with 'three retries at each layer' and states that 'the load on the database will increase 243x, making it unlikely to ever recover'; the article's own walk-through counts 'first three tries, then nine tries', and 243 is 3 to the fifth, so the multiplier is three attempts per layer. For low-cost control-plane and data-plane operations it states that 'our best practice is to retry at a single point in the stack'.

The Amazon Builders' Library describes a local token bucket for retries: calls may retry while tokens remain, then retry at a fixed rate once tokens run out, and states that AWS added this behaviour to the AWS SDK in 2016.

The Amazon Builders' Library states that APIs with side effects are not safe to retry unless they provide idempotency, and names Amazon EC2's RunInstances token-based idempotency as the mechanism that makes a creation call retryable.

The Amazon Builders' Library argues that 'circuit breakers introduce modal behavior into systems that can be difficult to test' and can significantly lengthen recovery time, and presents the token bucket as a lower-risk alternative.
The Amazon Builders' Library notes that eventual consistency blurs the retry classification boundary, because a client error can become a success once state propagates.

The 2015 AWS Architecture Blog simulation of optimistic concurrency control (network delay with a 10 ms mean and 4 ms variance) found that with no backoff, completion time grows linearly with contention while total work grows as the square of the number of clients in that simulated contention model, and that capped exponential backoff alone reduced client work only slightly.
In the same 2015 simulation, adding jitter at 100 contending clients cut the number of calls by more than half against un-jittered capped exponential backoff and also improved completion time.

The 2015 AWS Architecture Blog comparison of jitter variants found full jitter and equal jitter making roughly the same number of calls, decorrelated jitter making more, and equal jitter doing slightly more work than full while taking much longer; no variant changes the squared growth of total work with contention in that simulated model.
The 2015 AWS Architecture Blog post was updated in May 2023 with a note that most AWS SDKs now support exponential backoff and jitter in their standard and adaptive retry modes.

Google's SRE book describes client-side adaptive throttling in which each client tracks requests and accepts over the last two minutes and starts rejecting requests locally once requests reach K times accepts; the authors say they generally prefer the 2x multiplier.
Google's SRE book sets a per-request limit of three attempts and a per-client rule that retries continue only while they make up less than 10 percent of that client's requests.

Google's SRE book states that in the worst case, where a datacenter accepts few requests and rejects most, the three-attempt per-request limit alone pushes that client's total attempted traffic to just under 3 times its request rate, and that adding the 10 percent per-client retry budget reduces the growth of that client's own traffic to about 1.1 times; the figure bounds one client at one layer and is not a composition across layers.

Google's SRE book states that requests should only be retried at the layer immediately above the layer that is rejecting them, to prevent a combinatorial retry explosion across a deep dependency stack.

gRPC's retry design (gRFC A6, last updated 2024-08-23) throttles retries with a per-server-name token bucket: token_count starts at maxTokens (an integer in the range 0 to 1000 exclusive of 0), each failed RPC decrements it by 1, each successful RPC increments it by tokenRatio, and retries stop while token_count is at or below maxTokens/2.

In gRPC's retry design, only failures with retryable or non-fatal status codes, or pushback saying not to retry, decrement the throttling token count; errors such as INVALID_ARGUMENT do not count against it.

gRPC's client-side maximum is 5 attempts: 'Values greater than 5 are treated as 5 without being considered a validation error', and 'This client-side maximum value can be changed by the client through the use of channel arguments'. A retry policy itself comes from the service config rather than being on by default.

gRPC's backoff formula applies jitter unconditionally and outside the cap: the first retry waits initialBackoff x random(0.8, 1.2) and the nth waits min(initialBackoff x backoffMultiplier^(n-1), maxBackoff) x random(0.8, 1.2), so maxBackoff is a pre-jitter cap and the document notes the delay may be slightly lower than initialBackoff or slightly higher than maxBackoff.

gRPC lets a server override the client ladder with the grpc-retry-pushback-ms metadata key, an ASCII signed 32-bit integer: the client retries after exactly that many milliseconds, a negative or unparseable value means do not retry, and after a pushback later retries reset to initialBackoff unless pushback is received again.

gRPC's hedging policy sends the original RPC immediately and another hedge after each hedgingDelay without a response up to maxAttempts; a non-fatal error sends the next hedge immediately, a fatal error cancels all outstanding RPCs, and hedges are sent only while the throttling token count is above the threshold, though the first RPC is always sent.
gRPC's retry design recommends listing in retryableStatusCodes only codes indicating the server did not process the request, leaving more aggressive lists to the service owner for idempotent methods.

gRFC A6 states that 'gRPC's call deadline applies across all attempts for a given RPC' and that once the deadline passes the operation fails 'regardless of how many attempts were configured or attempted'; for hedging, 'As with retries, gRPC call deadlines apply to the entire chain of hedged requests', and transparent retries of RPCs that never left the client continue 'until a success occurs, or the RPC's deadline passes'.

gRFC A6 does not state what happens when a call deadline expires during a backoff delay, and its pushback section does not mention deadlines, so whether a server-requested delay that runs past the deadline is honoured or cut short is not settled by the document (read 2026-10-14).

The AWS SDK reference page for the 2026 retry behaviour opens with the gate: 'The behavior described on this page requires opting in until it becomes the default behavior. Set AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true in your environment', and states that without the setting the SDK uses pre-2026 retry behaviour differing in backoff timing, quota costs and service-specific defaults (read 2026-10-14).

The 2026 AWS SDK retry behaviour classifies each failed request as transient, throttling or non-retryable from the error code first and the HTTP status code second, so an HTTP 400 with RequestTimeout is retried while an HTTP 400 with ValidationException is returned immediately.

The documented status-code fallback in the 2026 AWS SDK retry behaviour is narrow: the transient class lists the error codes RequestTimeout, RequestTimeoutException, InternalError, IDPCommunicationError and I/O failures, plus '(any HTTP 500, 502, 503, or 504 without a recognized error code)'; the throttling class is a list of 14 error codes (Throttling, ThrottlingException, ThrottledException, RequestThrottledException, TooManyRequestsException, ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, TransactionInProgressException, LimitExceededException, PriorRequestNotComplete, RequestThrottled, EC2ThrottledException, RequestLimitExceeded, SlowDown, BandwidthLimitExceeded) with no documented status-code fallback of its own (read 2026-10-14).

The 2026 AWS SDK retry behaviour uses a base delay of 50 ms for transient errors and 1,000 ms for throttling errors, and computes each delay as random(0, 1) x min(20,000 ms, base_delay x 2^retry), full jitter with a 20-second cap.
Under the 2026 AWS SDK retry behaviour an HTTP 5XX carrying a throttling error code is classified as throttling rather than transient, because the SDK matches on error code before HTTP status.

The 2026 AWS SDK default is 3 max attempts (one initial request and two retries), with max_attempts set to 1 to disable retries; DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams clients default to 4 attempts with a 25 ms transient base delay instead of 50 ms.

The AWS SDK's own worked examples put the added latency of the default 3 attempts at about 75 ms on average for a transient error (two retries averaging 25 ms and 50 ms) and about 1,500 ms for a throttling error, and note that with the default of 3 max attempts the 20-second backoff cap is never reached (read 2026-10-14).

The 2026 AWS SDK retry quota is a 500-token budget in which a transient retry costs 14 tokens and a throttling retry costs 5; a successful retry restores only its own cost, a first-try success restores 1 token, and at zero the SDK returns errors without retrying.

AWS documents that with the default 3 max attempts the retry quota begins to drain above roughly 22 percent sustained transient failures or roughly 32 percent throttling failures, and that the 500-token starting balance absorbs short bursts without blocking retries.

AWS states the higher transient token cost (14 against 5) is deliberate: transient errors such as 500s and connection failures often indicate a service-wide problem where continued retrying is unlikely to succeed, while throttling signals that the service needs more time.

Some AWS services return an x-amz-retry-after header in milliseconds; the SDK uses that server-specified delay clamped between the computed backoff and the computed backoff plus 5,000 ms, applies no jitter of its own because the service is expected to jitter it, and the effective maximum is therefore 25 seconds.

For long-polling AWS operations (SQS.ReceiveMessage, SFN.GetActivityTask, SWF.PollForActivityTask, SWF.PollForDecisionTask) the SDK still applies a backoff delay before returning the error when the retry quota is depleted, because those calls sit in tight loops that would otherwise spin.

AWS documents that adaptive retry mode adds a per-client-instance rate limiter that can delay or block the initial request, is not recommended as a general default, and slows all requests from a client when one resource is throttled.
The AWS SDK retry quota's token budget is typically scoped to a single SDK client instance and is not shared across processes or hosts.

AWS announced the updated SDK retry behaviour on 2026-05-20 as opt-in through the environment variable AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026, to become the default in November 2026, after which the flag is ignored and reverting requires overriding individual settings.

AWS states that before the 2026 change each SDK used a single base delay for all error types, ranging from 10 ms to 1,000 ms across SDKs, that the transient retry cost rose from 5 to 14 tokens, and that the first retry after a brief 503 now averages about 25 ms rather than hundreds of milliseconds.

AWS gives as its reasons for the 2026 retry change that defaults varied across SDKs, that some waited too long before retrying transient errors while others kept retrying instead of failing fast during sustained outages, and that retry traffic from many clients can delay recovery.

Envoy's retry budget bounds retries as concurrency rather than count: budget_percent defaults to 20 percent of active plus active pending requests, min_retry_concurrency defaults to 3, and setting retry_budget overrides the max_retries circuit breaker, whose own default is 3 parallel retries (Envoy docs build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06, read 2026-10-14).
Envoy documents that when a retry budget replaces max_retries, the remaining retry capacity is no longer tracked in stats (docs build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06, read 2026-10-14).

Envoy's outlier detection defaults eject a host after 5 consecutive 5xx responses, check every 10 s, eject for a base of 30 s, never eject more than 10 percent of hosts, and cap ejection at 300 s (Envoy docs build 1.41.0-dev-35ef06, read 2026-10-14).

Envoy's success-rate outlier detection requires at least 100 requests per host (success_rate_request_volume) across at least 5 hosts (success_rate_minimum_hosts) and uses a standard-deviation factor of 1900/1000, that is 1.9; failure-percentage enforcement is off by default (enforcing_failure_percentage 0) while consecutive-5xx and success-rate enforcement are at 100 (read 2026-10-14).

Envoy's ejection time is base_ejection_time multiplied by the number of consecutive times the host has been ejected, capped at max_ejection_time, and the multiplier decreases one step per check interval while the host stays healthy, so recovery to the base time takes about max_ejection_time / base_ejection_time x interval seconds (read 2026-10-14).
Envoy documents that an ejected host is skipped by load balancing only outside panic mode: in a panic scenario the load balancer can still route to ejected hosts (read 2026-10-14).

Envoy's panic threshold defaults to 50 percent of healthy hosts: below that share Envoy stops using health status and balances across all hosts, or none, depending on the configured mode, and the mechanism exists to 'avoid a situation in which host failures cascade throughout the cluster as load increases' (read 2026-10-14).

Envoy documents that failing traffic can itself reduce load on a struggling upstream, at the cost of requests that never succeed, and that setting the panic threshold to 0 percent disables panic mode for a priority level (read 2026-10-14).

Resilience4j's documented circuit breaker has three normal states (CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN) and three special ones (METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED, FORCED_OPEN), the last of which always rejects calls (docs read 2026-10-14; latest release listed as v2.4.0).

Resilience4j's documented circuit breaker defaults are a count-based sliding window of 100 calls, a failureRateThreshold of 50 percent, a minimumNumberOfCalls of 100 before the rate is evaluated, a waitDurationInOpenState of 60,000 ms, a slowCallDurationThreshold of 60,000 ms and a slowCallRateThreshold of 100 percent; in half-open it permits 10 calls and evaluates their failure and slow-call rates against the same thresholds rather than requiring all 10 to pass (docs read 2026-10-14).
Resilience4j's automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled defaults to false, so an open breaker moves to half-open only when a call is attempted rather than on a timer (docs read 2026-10-14).

Resilience4j's documented retry defaults are maxAttempts 3 and a constant waitDuration of 500 ms with no randomization; exponential and randomized ladders are opt-in through IntervalFunction.ofExponentialBackoff() and IntervalFunction.ofRandomized() (docs read 2026-10-14).
The latest resilience4j release listed on its GitHub releases page on 2026-10-14 is v2.4.0.

Polly's documented circuit breaker defaults are a FailureRatio of 0.1 (10 percent), a MinimumThroughput of 100 executions, a SamplingDuration of 30 seconds and a BreakDuration of 5 seconds; if MinimumThroughput is not reached within the sampling duration the failure ratio is ignored and the circuit does not break, so Polly cannot open below 100 calls per 30 seconds while resilience4j opens only after 100 recorded calls however long they take (docs read 2026-10-14).

Polly documents that its circuit breaker runs no background timer: the move from Open to HalfOpen happens only when an Execute method is called, so an application that calls Execute only when the circuit is closed never reaches HalfOpen and never probes (docs read 2026-10-14).

Polly's documented retry defaults are MaxRetryAttempts 3, Delay 2 seconds, BackoffType Constant, MaxDelay null and UseJitter false, so jitter is opt-in; when enabled with exponential backoff the implementation is the Decorrelated Jitter Backoff V2 formula from Polly.Contrib.WaitAndRetry (docs read 2026-10-14; latest release listed as 8.8.0).
The latest Polly release listed on its GitHub releases page on 2026-10-14 is 8.8.0.

RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, June 2022) says servers send Retry-After 'to indicate how long the user agent ought to wait', defines the value as either an HTTP-date or delay-seconds ('a non-negative decimal integer, representing time in seconds'), and gives its meaning for 503 ('how long the service is expected to be unavailable to the client') and for 3xx ('the minimum time that the user agent is asked to wait before issuing the redirected request'); section 10.2.3 does not mention 429, and only the 3xx case states a wait the client is asked to observe.

RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 states that 'Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response', that 'A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent, regardless of the method, or some means to detect that the original request was never applied', and that 'A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests.'

RFC 6585 (April 2012) defines 429 Too Many Requests and says the response MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait, so a rate-limited client has no guarantee of being told when to return.

The IETF RateLimit header fields draft defines a RateLimit field whose r parameter is the remaining quota and whose t parameter is the effective window in seconds (an integer rather than a timestamp, which avoids clock-sync problems), plus a RateLimit-Policy field with q, qu, w and pk parameters that clients MAY ignore (draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-11, 2026-05-23).

The IETF RateLimit header fields draft states that when a response carries both RateLimit and Retry-After, the Retry-After field MUST take precedence, and that the spec mandates no retry or backoff algorithm (draft 11, 2026-05-23).

The IETF RateLimit header fields draft says the delay-seconds form of the effective window mitigates the risk related to thundering herd compared with timestamps, and its security section warns that many throttled clients would otherwise return at the same moment, giving a daily 18:00:00 reset as the example and suggesting jitter on the effective window as the mitigation (draft 11, section 8.5, 2026-05-23).

The IETF RateLimit header fields draft tells clients not to treat a positive remaining quota as a guarantee that requests will succeed, not to assume the full limit is restored when the effective window ends, and to set their own thresholds against excessive server-advertised values, for example handling effective windows longer than ten minutes differently (draft 11, 2026-05-23).

Searched the IETF Datatracker document page for the RateLimit header fields on 2026-10-14: the work is still an active Internet-Draft at revision 11 (2026-05-23), IESG state 'I-D Exists', expiring 2026-11-24, so no published RFC standardizes these fields as of that date.

Searched the IETF Datatracker for the Idempotency-Key header work on 2026-10-14: the httpapi draft, whose abstract offers fault tolerance for non-idempotent methods such as POST and PATCH, reached revision 07 on 2025-10-15 and its IESG state is 'Expired', so the replay-safety field a client would use to make a write retryable has no finished standard.

The kubelet's CrashLoopBackOff ladder grows exponentially from 10 s through 20 s and 40 s, is capped at five minutes, and resets only after a container has run for 10 minutes (twice the maximum) without problems (KEP-4603, SIG Node).

KEP-4603's benchmark of 110 instantly crashing single-container pods on one node saw /pods API traffic peak near the kubelet's roughly 5 QPS client limit before settling around 2 QPS, with runtime CPU about 10 times higher, kubelet CPU about twice, and API server CPU about twice.

KEP-4603 proposes cutting the kubelet's initial restart delay from 10 s to 1 s and the maximum from 5 minutes to 1 minute, and models the cost of that change as about 5 extra restarts per crashing pod in the first five minutes and about 5 more every five minutes after that, and roughly 10 times more pod state-transition API requests at peak on a fully saturated node (about 2,750 excess requests in total); the modelled request estimate is separate from the measured QPS benchmark on 110 pods.

KEP-4603 argues that exponential decay mainly protects against unrecoverable failures that could overload the kubelet, that frequent restarts can starve the kubelet and in extreme cases crash nodes, and that some throttling or quota for restarts is always needed to protect node stability.

KEP-5593 keeps the default kubelet restart curve unchanged (10 s initial, doubling to a 300 s cap) and lets operators opt into a per-node maximum between 1 and 300 seconds behind the KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax gate; values outside the range fail validation and the kubelet will not start.

KEP-5593 records that a stress test with a 0 second maximum raised API server QPS up to 30 times and roughly doubled kubelet CPU, which is why 0 was ruled invalid, and that at a 1 second maximum a fully saturated node is estimated to make roughly 10 times more pod state-transition API requests.

The shipped KubeletConfiguration reference (kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1) spells the setting as a crashLoopBackOff field of type CrashLoopBackOffConfig holding maxContainerRestartPeriod, a meta/v1.Duration documented as 'the maximum duration the backoff delay can accrue to for container restarts, minimum 1 second, maximum 300 seconds. If not set, defaults to the internal crashloopbackoff maximum (300s)'; the reference section names no feature gate (read 2026-10-14).

The Kubernetes feature gates reference lists two separate features: KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax, which lets an operator configure the maximum restart delay, was alpha and off by default from 1.32 to 1.34 and is beta and on by default since 1.35, while ReduceDefaultCrashLoopBackOffDecay, which cuts the cluster-wide defaults, is alpha and off by default since 1.33 (read 2026-10-14).

The Kubernetes feature gates reference describes ReduceDefaultCrashLoopBackOffDecay as enabling 'reduction of both the initial delay and the maximum delay accrued between container restarts for a node for containers in CrashLoopBackOff across the cluster to 1s initial delay and 60s maximum delay' (read 2026-10-14).

The OSDI '22 study page credits the metastable-failure framework to prior work ('Recently, Bronson et al. introduced a framework for understanding a class of failures in distributed systems') and says the authors 'extend the model by Bronson et al.' by 'categorizing two types of triggers and two types of amplification mechanisms', so retry machinery is one amplification mechanism among others rather than the only one (abstract read 2026-10-14).

The OSDI '22 study examined public incident reports and presents 'an in-depth study of 22 metastable failures from 11 different organizations', and reports that 'at least 4 out of 15 major outages in the last decade at Amazon Web Services were caused by metastable failures'.

The framework the OSDI '22 study extends is Nathan Bronson, Abutalib Aghayev, Aleksey Charapko and Timothy Zhu, 'Metastable failures in distributed systems', HotOS 2021 (18th Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems), ACM, pages 221 to 227, doi 10.1145/3458336.3465286, published 2021-06-01; the record describes a paper that introduces the framework, applies it to examples from operating large-scale distributed systems, and leaves robustness to unknown metastable failures as an open problem (bibliographic record read 2026-10-14; the paper PDF has no extractable text layer and the ACM page returns 403).

Marc Brooker's 2021 post on metastability states the model as 'a trigger causes the system to enter a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed', names a short failure, a load spike and a deployment as example triggers, and holds that 'We consider the root cause of a metastable failure to be the sustaining feedback loop, rather than the trigger'; he describes the resulting 'stable down' state in which clients keep sending work and goodput is zero.

The same post names retries as a mechanism that makes systems more vulnerable by 'converting small outages into sudden (and metastable) periods of internal retry storms', and warns that adding retries can lower the everyday error rate while raising exposure to that failure mode.

Marc Brooker argues that circuit breakers do not solve retry-driven overload in sharded or cell-based systems because failure there is partial: a breaker that trips on one overloaded shard's failures also hurts customers of the healthy shards, and one that does not trip does nothing useful (2022-02-16).

Brooker's objection rests on a client's epistemic limit: a client cannot reliably predict whether a specific call with specific parameters will succeed, and should not need to know the server's internals to decide (2022-02-16).

Brooker names two benefits circuit breakers do deliver, failing early to avoid spending resources on calls that will fail, and progressive degradation that drops optional features whose backing service is down, and three fixes with costs: clients that know the sharding scheme, servers that signal overload per key range, and statistical inference (2022-02-16).

Brooker's simulation of one randomly failing service with 100 independent clients sending Poisson arrivals found that three retries is the most robust option but the most expensive, costing 1+N (four) times the work at a 100 percent failure rate (2022-02-28).
In that main 100-client model, 'the breaker strategy starts tripping a little early: around half the expected rate', because each client samples failures independently (2022-02-28).

Repeating the same total request rate split across 10, 100 and 1,000 clients, Brooker reports that the circuit breaker 'is tripping too early, and approaching the performance of the no retries approach' while the token bucket 'doesn't deplete its bucket fast enough, converging on the behavior of n retries' (2022-02-28).

Brooker's token-bucket scheme deposits a fraction of a token (for example 0.1) per successful call and spends a whole token per retry, so it behaves like N retries at low failure rates and like about 0.1 retries at high ones; of it he writes 'The adaptive strategy isn't modal in the same way, and seems to perform better at lower failure rates, but does give some (tunable) additional load at higher rates', and summarizes the goal as throttling yourself before you DoS yourself (2022-02-28).

A 2026-08-26 arXiv preprint surveying 200 open-source Python microservice projects detected explicit retry logic in 11.5 percent of them, and its authors estimate true prevalence near 41 percent after auditing their own false negatives.

In the same 2026 survey, 60.9 percent of the projects where retry logic was detected carried at least one configuration with no backoff at all, and exactly 1 of 113 manually verified production retry configurations randomized its delay.

The preprint's conclusion is that retry behaviour should be designed as a system-level property rather than configured locally at each call site, and it catalogues five recurring anti-patterns alongside its retry amplification factor metric for the extra request volume retries create during partial failures.

In the preprint's hardest scenario (S3), with 100 trials per configuration, success rates were 55.4 percent with no retries, 41.5 percent for Standard Retry, 55.3 percent for Standard Retry plus a circuit breaker, and 54.9 percent for the authors' Adaptive Retry Budgeting; retry amplification factors were 1.34 for Standard Retry against 1.00 for no retries, 1.00 for the breaker and 1.01 for budgeting (full text read 2026-10-14).

The preprint's Standard Retry baseline is 3 attempts with exponential backoff of 100, 200 and 400 ms plus jitter; its circuit breaker is that same policy plus a breaker that trips at a 50 percent failure rate and stays open 30 seconds; its Adaptive Retry Budgeting starts from a budget of 0.2 of base load with alpha 0.1, beta 0.5, thresholds 0.3 and 0.05, a 1.0 second window and backpressure above 80 percent queue occupancy or 90 percent CPU (full text read 2026-10-14).

The preprint's own limits section records that every simulated number comes from one 5-tier linear chain (API, Auth, Catalog, Inventory, Database) at 50 percent baseline utilization with an idealized network and independently injected failures, covers synchronous request and response only, and that its analytical amplification bound of 10.30x against a simulated 1.34x should not be read as a forecast (full text read 2026-10-14).

AWS's summary of the October 2025 us-east-1 disruption records that a DNS Enactor delayed while retrying endpoint updates 'applied its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan', that 'The second Enactor's clean-up process then deleted this older plan because it was many generations older than the plan it had just applied', and that 'As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed'; the event began 2025-10-19 at 23:48 PDT and ended 2025-10-20 at 14:20 PDT.

In the same event, AWS records that DWFM 'had entered a state of congestive collapse and was unable to make forward progress in recovering droplet leases', with 'Additional work was queued to reattempt establishing the droplet lease' and lease attempts timing out, and that engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts at 04:14 PDT on 2025-10-20; the summary states that the DNS Enactor 'will retry each endpoint until the plan is successfully applied' but gives no retry interval, spacing or backoff anywhere (read 2026-10-14).

AWS's remediation for the October 2025 us-east-1 event includes improving the throttling mechanism in its EC2 data propagation systems to 'rate limit incoming work based on the size of the waiting queue'; the published remediation list does not name retries or backoff directly.

AWS also records that alternating NLB health check results increased load on the health check subsystem during the October 2025 event, and that Lambda Event Source Mappings and asynchronous invocations were throttled to protect synchronous invocations.

OpenTelemetry's HTTP span conventions define one stable retry signal, http.request.resend_count, 'the ordinal number of request resending attempt (for any reason, including redirects)', recommended if and only if the request was retried and counted regardless of cause, including redirects, authorization challenges, 503 responses and network issues (read 2026-10-14, links pointing to specification v1.59.0).

Searched OpenTelemetry's HTTP metrics semantic conventions page for 'resend', 'retry' and 'attempt' on 2026-10-14: none appears. The six HTTP client metrics defined there (request.duration, request.body.size, response.body.size, open_connections, connection.duration, active_requests) carry no retry attribute, and the page does not say whether http.client.request.duration includes time spent on retries.

Outside the HTTP conventions, gRPC's OpenTelemetry metrics are measured per attempt as well as per call: grpc.client.attempt.started, grpc.client.attempt.duration and the two attempt message-size histograms are stable and on by default beside the stable per-call grpc.client.call.duration (read 2026-10-14).

gRPC additionally defines four per-call retry instruments, grpc.client.call.retries, grpc.client.call.transparent_retries, grpc.client.call.hedges and grpc.client.call.retry_delay, all marked experimental, and states that 'Experimental metrics are always off by default' (read 2026-10-14).

Temporal's default retry policy for Activities is a 1 second initial interval, a backoff coefficient of 2.0, a maximum interval of 100 times the initial interval and unlimited maximum attempts; Activities retry automatically while Workflow Executions have no retry policy by default (docs read 2026-10-14).

Temporal retries Workflow Task Executions outside the retry policy, with exponential backoff capped at 10 minutes, until the Workflow Execution Timeout, which is unlimited by default (docs read 2026-10-14).

Temporal matches non-retryable errors on the type field of an Application Failure, and an error flagged non-retryable in code (non_retryable=True in Python, nonRetryable: true in TypeScript, newNonRetryableFailure() in Java, NewNonRetryableApplicationError() in Go) is always non-retryable regardless of the retry policy; the docs advise using this sparingly, mainly for permanent failures such as bad input (read 2026-10-14).

Temporal keeps Activity attempts out of Event History until the Activity completes or fails after exhausting retries, exposing the attempt count for a pending Activity through the Describe API; a failed Workflow run with a retry policy records a retry state of IN_PROGRESS with the next run's ID and the backoff duration (read 2026-10-14).

Netflix's Hystrix repository states that 'Hystrix is no longer in active development, and is currently in maintenance mode', names 1.5.18 as the final release, points new internal projects at resilience4j, and says Netflix has shifted toward more adaptive implementations that react to an application's real-time performance, such as adaptive concurrency limits (read 2026-10-14).

Amazon SQS moves a message to a dead-letter queue once it has been received maxReceiveCount times without being deleted, and warns that a low value such as 1 dead-letters a message after a single failed receive; the docs advise setting it high enough to allow sufficient retries (read 2026-10-14).

Both libraries wait for a caller to supply the probe: the clock makes an open breaker eligible for half-open, and an arriving call makes the transition happen. [11] , [14]
Ejection escalates per host and unwinds on a clock, which is the part a fleet-wide trip cannot do: the penalty is proportional to one host's record and bounded to a tenth of the fleet. [9] , [10]
